class.name: PhysXWaterSurface3D
class.brief_description: A real animated water surface: a GPU FFT ocean spectrum layer plus a local ripple layer that bodies can disturb, rendered as a displaced mesh.
class.description: Two coupled simulation layers, both real-time GPU compute through the shared main [RenderingDevice] when windowed: a local iWave-style ripple layer (a damped 2D wave equation you can disturb via [method submit_sphere]/[method submit_impulse]) and a Tessendorf FFT ocean spectrum layer (large-scale wind-driven chop, tuned by [member wind_speed]/[member wind_direction]/[member wave_amplitude]). Rendering also produces optional light-space caustics with a direct [RenderingDevice] graphics pass; it does not create a second [SubViewport]. A child [MeshInstance3D] (a subdivided [PlaneMesh], sized to [member ocean_domain_size], or the resampled [member surface_mesh] footprint) is created automatically and displaced by both layers, summed. Call [method sample_height] to query the same combined surface on the CPU -- e.g. from a buoyancy script (see [code]demo/common/buoyant_body.gd[/code] in the paired demo project) -- and [method submit_sphere] once per physics tick per floating body so it actually disturbs the ripple layer, not just receives a height back. No [RenderingDevice] compute support (e.g. running headless) leaves the surface flat and [method sample_height] returning [member water_level] plus zero -- a graceful no-op, not an error, matching every other GPU solver in this module. Set [member surface_mesh] to give the water any outline -- a round pool, a kidney-bean pond, a lake with an island. Waves reflect off its shoreline, and [method sample_height]/[method is_wet] report no water outside it. Set [member seabed_from_floor] for water over uneven ground -- a beach, a lake bed. The still-water depth of every ripple cell is then measured from the floor: waves travel at the local shallow-water speed, so they slow and bunch up over shallows, the shoreline falls wherever the ground rises above the water, and the ocean chop fades out over the last [member shallow_fade_depth] meters. Without it, the whole surface uses the constant [member depth]. [PhysXWaterWake3D] nodes on moving bodies draw their wakes and foam on the surface (up to four), and [method sample_height] includes them. Both simulation grids are centered on the node's global position (plus the [member surface_mesh] footprint's center), fixed when the node enters the tree or a property changes. The node's rotation and scale are not applied to the simulation, so keep it unrotated and unscaled. Only runs in an actual running game, never in the editor -- placing or moving the node in the Inspector does not simulate.

method.name: clear_inflow
method.description: Removes the inflow [param owner] registered with [method set_inflow].

method.name: clear_outflow
method.description: Removes the outlet registered by [param owner] (see [method set_outflow]).

method.name: clear_sphere
method.description: Removes a previously-submitted sphere proxy (see [method submit_sphere]) by its owner id. Call this when a floating body leaves the water or is freed; a proxy left in place otherwise keeps disturbing the ripple layer at its last submitted position.

method.name: get_breaker_stats
method.description: The plunging lips of the last tick: [code]crest_points[/code], [code]vertices[/code], [code]triangles[/code], [code]spray_rate[/code] (droplets per second) and [code]cpu_ms[/code] (time to build them).

method.name: get_caustics_half_extent
method.description: Half-width of the square light-space projection in world units, used to map receiver positions to [method get_caustics_texture] UV coordinates.

method.name: get_caustics_light_right
method.description: Light-space horizontal projection axis used to sample [method get_caustics_texture].

method.name: get_caustics_light_up
method.description: Light-space vertical projection axis used to sample [method get_caustics_texture].

method.name: get_caustics_origin
method.description: World-space center of the light-space caustics projection.

method.name: get_caustics_texture
method.description: The zero-copy caustics light-pattern texture. Project a receiving surface's world position onto [method get_caustics_light_right] and [method get_caustics_light_up], relative to [method get_caustics_origin], and map the result through [method get_caustics_half_extent] to sample the texture. A half-float texture. Red is the sun's irradiance at [member caustics_reference_depth] over what a flat surface lets through (1 even light, 0 none, above 1 at a focus, up to 64), already multiplied by green; green is 1 where the sun ray through that spot crossed the water's surface over water and 0 where it didn't. Use [code]red + (1 - green)[/code] as the factor on the sun's light, so the outside of a pool's wall, which lines up with lit spots inside the pool, stays evenly lit. Past the simulated square, light counts as coming through water only when the surface is rendered out there ([member render_extent]). Null until [member caustics_enabled] is true and the node has built.

method.name: get_caustics_tile_size
method.description: The caustics repeat with the ocean waves, every [member ocean_domain_size]. A receiver can fold its world XZ into the tile around [method get_caustics_origin] ([code]p -= tile * round((p - origin) / tile)[/code]) before projecting, so caustics reach the whole seabed -- all along a beach -- not just the simulated square. The map spans a little more than one tile, so there's no seam.

method.name: get_contact_foam_cells
method.description: Cells of the last contact map with a contact foam ring on the water (benches and tests).

method.name: get_contact_foam_rays
method.description: Rays the last contact map took (a coarse pass, then the full resolution only near the waterline).

method.name: get_crest_sheet_count
method.description: Torn spray sheets alive at the last physics tick (see [member crest_sheets]).

method.name: get_crest_spray_rate
method.description: Droplets a second leaving the open sea's crests at the last update of [member crest_spray] (0 when off, calm or out of reach).

method.name: get_detail_slope_variance
method.description: Mean square slope of the [member detail_waves] band, from the Phillips saturation range of the sea's JONSWAP spectrum ([code]alpha / 2 ln(k2 / k1)[/code], alpha from the fetch). Where a pixel is too large to show those waves this variance is added to the water's roughness instead.

method.name: get_detail_wave_tile
method.description: Side of the [member detail_waves] tile in metres: its band starts where the finest cascade's grid stops.

method.name: get_effective_fetch
method.description: The fetch (meters of open water the wind blows over) the wave spectrum actually uses: [member fetch] when it's above 0, otherwise the automatic value -- the longest side of the [member surface_mesh] footprint for enclosed water, or 100 km (a fully developed open sea) for the plain square.

method.name: get_effective_foam_threshold
method.description: The foam threshold in use: [member foam_threshold], or with [member whitecap_auto] on, the threshold steered to the wind's whitecap cover.

method.name: get_outflow_discharge
method.description: What the outlets pass at the current level (m³/s).

method.name: get_wave_cascade_size
method.description: The tile size of wave cascade [param index]: [member ocean_domain_size] times [member wave_cascade_ratio] to the power [param index].

method.name: get_whitecap_cover
method.description: The share of the sea under whitecap foam (0 to 1) at the last readback of the foam grids, or [code]-1[/code] before the first one.

method.name: get_whitecap_target_cover
method.description: The whitecap cover the wind asks for with [member whitecap_auto]: [code]3.84e-6 * wind_speed^3.41[/code] (Monahan and O'Muircheartaigh 1980) times [member whitecap_cover_scale], at most [code]0.5[/code].

method.name: is_camera_underwater
method.description: Whether the active camera was under the surface (by [method sample_height] at the camera) when the node last updated the underwater view. Always [code]false[/code] while [member underwater_enabled] is off or the camera is out of reach of the water.

method.name: is_contact_foam_ready
method.description: True once a contact map has been measured and the water shows its contact foam.

method.name: is_ripple_resting
method.description: [code]true[/code] while the ripple layer is resting: [member ripple_rest_threshold] is set, it stayed flat for a few readbacks and nothing has disturbed it since, so its solve is skipped (see [member ripple_rest_threshold]).

method.name: is_wet
method.description: Whether there is water at [param world_pos]'s XZ, at the ripple grid's resolution: inside the [member surface_mesh] footprint, and not over dry seabed ([member seabed_from_floor]). With a [member render_extent] past the simulated square, the open water out to the edge of the rendered surface counts too, carrying on the seabed at the square's edge the way the surface is drawn (the sea side stays sea, a beach stays dry). [code]world_pos.y[/code] is ignored.

method.name: recenter
method.description: Moves the simulated ripple square to [param world_position]'s XZ (the node's height is kept), for a sea that follows the camera or the player. Unlike moving the node or changing [member domain_size], it doesn't rebuild the surface: the mesh, the textures and the FFT ocean (sampled in world space, so its waves stay where they are) carry on, and only the ripples are cleared -- no frame without water. A surface with a [member surface_mesh] footprint or a per-cell seabed ([member seabed_from_floor]) depends on where the square is, so it still rebuilds.

method.name: remeasure_contact_foam
method.description: Measures the contact map again over the next physics ticks (after bodies were added, moved or removed near the camera). The old map stays shown meanwhile.

method.name: remeasure_seabed
method.description: Measures the floor again for [member seabed_from_floor], when it changed at runtime: a dug channel, a raised sandbar, a wall that came down. The ripples, foam and swash carry on, and the waves, the shoreline and [method is_wet] follow the new floor. Changing [member seabed_from_floor] or [member seabed_collision_mask] rebuilds the surface instead, which clears them. The rays are cast on the next physics tick, one per ripple cell, so this costs that one tick more the larger [member grid_resolution] is; don't call it every tick. Needs [member seabed_from_floor].

method.name: sample_depth
method.description: Water depth in meters at [param world_pos]'s XZ: the surface as [method sample_height] reads it, over the seabed [member seabed_from_floor] measured (or [member depth] without one). Zero or below on dry ground. Safe from the physics thread.

method.name: sample_height
method.description: The combined surface height (ripple + ocean layers, plus [member water_level]) at [param world_pos]'s XZ, bilinearly sampled from the last readback (refreshed every physics tick, a few frames behind the GPU simulation -- fine for buoyancy, not meant for sub-frame precision), plus any [PhysXWaterWake3D] wakes there. [code]world_pos.y[/code] is ignored. Returns [code]-INF[/code] where [method is_wet] is [code]false[/code] (outside the [member surface_mesh] footprint, or over dry seabed), so anything comparing a point's height against it -- a buoyancy script's submersion depth -- reads "not in water" there. Past the simulated square (with a [member render_extent]) it is the FFT ocean, tiled, on still water -- the same surface that is drawn there, so bodies float on the open sea too.

method.name: sample_height_excluding_wake
method.description: The same as [method sample_height], but leaving out one [PhysXWaterWake3D]'s contribution (pass [code]null[/code] to leave out nothing). A boat that does its own buoyancy in a script should pass its own wake: otherwise it reads the dip and bow wave its hull pushes into the water and rides its own wake, sinking at the stern and pitching. Other boats' wakes are still included, so it still rocks on theirs. [PhysXBuoyancy3D] (and so [PhysXBoat3D]) already does this for a [PhysXWaterWake3D] that is another child of the same body.

method.name: sample_swash
method.description: The swash on the shore at [param world_pos]'s XZ: [code]x[/code] is the run-up film on the beach (meters of water over the ground above still water: the run-up's level less the ground's height there; 0 past where it reaches, and 0 below still water, where [method sample_depth] gives the depth), [code]y[/code] the wet sand (0 to 1: 1 under water and where the run-up reached, fading as it dries over [member wet_sand_dry_time]). Read back from the GPU every 8th water step (about 0.13 s behind); the first call turns that readback on, so it returns [code]Vector2(0, 0)[/code] until the first one lands, and outside the simulated square. Safe from the physics thread.

method.name: sample_vertical_speed
method.description: How fast the surface above [param world_pos]'s XZ is rising, in meters per second (negative while it falls): the ripple and ocean layers' change between the last two readbacks, so it is as far behind the GPU simulation as [method sample_height]. Wakes are left out. Returns [code]0.0[/code] where [method is_wet] is [code]false[/code], and until two readbacks have landed.

method.name: set_inflow
method.description: A river flowing in at [param at] (world, its mouth) heading along [param direction], [param width] metres wide and carrying [param discharge] m³/s. Its outflow spreads as a turbulent plane jet (Rajaratnam): a core about three widths long at the mouth speed, then slowing as the square root of the distance while it widens, worn down by the bed in shallow water. The plume is added to the flow over the simulated square, so the waves, foam and floating bodies ride it; the live water does not simulate it. [PhysXRiver3D] calls this for its [member PhysXRiver3D.mouth_target]; [param owner] identifies the inflow.

method.name: set_outflow
method.description: A river leaving this water at [param at] (world, its sill, whose top is at world height [param crest]) along [param direction] (out of the lake). The water drains over the sill as a broad-crested weir [param width] wide ([method weir_discharge]) and converges on it as a sink in a half plane, [code]Q / (pi r h)[/code] at distance r and depth h, added to the flow like the inflows' plumes (floating bodies and foam drift to the outlet). Called by [PhysXRiver3D] ([member PhysXRiver3D.source_lake]).

method.name: set_sea_state
method.description: Sets [member wind_speed], [member wind_direction], [member wave_amplitude] and [member fetch] at once. Once the surface is running, a change to any of them regenerates the wave spectrum in place: every wave keeps its phase and just grows, calms or turns, and the ripples, wakes and foam carry on -- so a storm can be ramped smoothly, every frame if needed. (Setting the four properties one by one does the same, with one update each.) Changing [member ocean_domain_size] still rebuilds the surface; don't animate it.

method.name: submit_impulse
method.description: A one-shot local disturbance (a splash) at [param world_pos]'s XZ -- consumed by the next simulation step, then cleared automatically. Call it once per event (e.g. on impact), not every tick.

method.name: submit_sphere
method.description: A persistent body proxy that pushes the ripple layer's surface down near [param world_pos]'s XZ, proportional to [param radius] and [param strength]. Call once per physics tick while a body is in the water (e.g. from its own [code]_physics_process[/code]), keyed by any id stable for that body's lifetime -- [code]get_instance_id()[/code] works well. Call [method clear_sphere] with the same id when the body leaves.

method.name: weir_discharge
method.description: The discharge (m³/s) over a broad-crested weir [param width] wide under [param head] metres of water: [code]Cd (2/3)^(3/2) b sqrt(g) H^(3/2)[/code] (critical depth on the crest; Henderson 1966).

members.member: With [member level_from_flows]: water reaching the lake besides the rivers flowing in (rain and springs of its catchment), m³/s.

Enables the light-space caustics draw pass and its render target. When disabled, the extra GPU buffers and draw are skipped. Clear water ([code]clear_water[/code] in the material) lights the bed it shows with it in the rasterizer: the sun's share of the bed's light is scaled by the map's ratio (the path tracer finds its own caustics). See [method get_caustics_texture]. Off by default: the pass draws every frame, and caustics only show over a floor seen through fairly shallow water (a pool, a beach, a lake shore), so turn it on where you have one.

Distance along the refracted light below the surface at which the caustics map is drawn: the depth where the pattern is sharpest (as HDRP's virtual plane distance). Beds much deeper than this fade to even light.

World-space direction that light travels from the source toward the water, used only while the scene has no visible [DirectionalLight3D] above the horizon (the map otherwise follows the light the water is drawn with). It need not be normalized.

Tessendorf horizontal displacement of the ocean layer: pulls the surface toward the wave crests so they sharpen and the troughs flatten, the way real wind waves look. [code]0[/code] is a pure height field; around [code]1[/code] is realistic, and much higher can fold the surface through itself. Fades out over the shallows with the rest of the ocean chop. Where the displacement folds the surface it also injects whitecap foam (see [member foam_threshold]). [method sample_height] accounts for the displacement.

Rock contact foam: a ring of white water where the sea meets a steep face (a sea stack, a boulder, a cliff foot), [member contact_foam_width] wide, widening as each crest arrives and drawing back in the trough, churned solid at the rock and lacy further out, plus wash over rock tops up to [member contact_foam_depth] under the surface. Read from a top-down height map of the static bodies in [member contact_foam_mask] over [member contact_foam_extent] round the camera, measured by rays (as the seabed is) and turned into the distance to the contact (an exact Euclidean distance transform) and the face's steepness there, so gentle beaches are left to the shore foam. The map is re-centred as the camera moves, spread over several physics ticks.
How deep under the surface (m) a rock top still washes white as crests pass over it. 0 = no wash, only the rings.
The side (m) of the square round the camera the contact map covers, at 0.25 m cells. Re-centred when the camera has moved an eighth of it.
Physics layers whose static bodies the contact map measures. Bodies that are not static (floaters, boats, players) are always stepped through.
The contact foam's opacity at the rock.
The contact foam ring's width (m) at mean water: it widens to about 1.6 times this under a crest and narrows to about half in a trough, with older, lacier foam out to three times it.

Where the sea reached stays wet in the weather's contact wetness ([code]WeatherMap3D.contact_wetness_enabled[/code]), so sand, rocks, plants and props on the shore stay dark and glossy up to where the waves ran and dry with the weather (much slower than [member wet_sand_dry_time], which is the sea's own wet sand). The swash's wetness is read back from the GPU every eighth step, over land and still water shallower than half a metre (piers and hulls over deeper water are left alone). Needs a varying depth ([member seabed_from_floor]).
Most [member crest_sheets] alive at once.

From a near-gale (12 m/s, fully by 20 m/s), thin sheets of water the wind tears off the open sea's strongest folding crests, 8 to 30 m from the camera: each flies downwind, curls over and falls back within about a second, tearing into streaks and ligaments as it goes (bag breakup, Troitskaya et al. 2017). Real geometry rebuilt each physics tick, so the path tracer draws it too.

Spray torn off breaking crests by the wind (spume): droplets leave the open sea where the surface folds (the same test as the whitecaps) once [member wind_speed] passes about 9 m/s, rising to full by 20 m/s, and fly downwind. Emitted within 40 m of the camera, not nearer than 8 m, and drawn like the surf's spray, with soft puffs of fine spume (an eighth as many, a few metres across, kept low and blown along) so the spray reads as white smoke off each crest. The emitters are found on the CPU from the ocean's readback every fourth physics tick.
Most [member crest_spray] droplets alive at once (the spume puffs are an eighth of this).

Extra room (m) added around the surface before it is culled. The surface's bounds already allow for 4 times [member wave_amplitude], or 2 m if that is larger. Raise this for a material that displaces the surface further, such as a whirlpool or a tsunami wall, if the water disappears at grazing angles. A larger margin draws the water more often when it is off-screen.
Damping (ALPHA) on the local ripple layer's wave equation -- higher settles disturbances faster.

Still-water depth in meters used everywhere unless [member seabed_from_floor] measures it per cell (then it only applies where no floor is found below the water). Sets the ripple layer's wave speed, [code]sqrt(g * depth)[/code], and the ocean layer's dispersion and spectrum: in shallow water the long waves carry less energy (TMA spectrum), so set it to the real depth of open water (tens of meters for a sea).

Short waves the finest cascade's grid cannot carry (from its Nyquist wavelength down to about 8 cm), on a small FFT tile of their own, for the per-pixel normals, and displaced into the open sea mesh near the camera (see [member near_mesh_step]): crests get their ripples and glitter. Where they are smaller than a pixel they fade out and their slope variance goes to the roughness (Bruneton, Neyret and Holzschuch 2010), so the far sea keeps its glitter without shimmering. One more 128² FFT a step.

World-space extent (X, Z) of the local ripple layer -- independent of [member ocean_domain_size], see [member ocean_grid_resolution]'s own note on why. Ignored when [member surface_mesh] is set: the ripple grid is then fitted to the footprint's bounds.

How far the wind has blown over open water, in meters. The ocean layer is a fetch-limited JONSWAP spectrum, so fetch sets how tall and how long the wind waves get at a given [member wind_speed]: a few meters give tiny, short ripples, kilometers give a developed sea. [code]0[/code] (auto) uses the [member surface_mesh] footprint's longest side for enclosed water, or a fully developed open sea (100 km) without one. Only wavelengths up to [member ocean_domain_size] are represented, and waves shorter than two ocean grid cells aren't, so a small fetch at a coarse [member ocean_grid_resolution] can leave the ocean layer flat.

Whether whitecap foam forms at all. Turn it off for water that should never show foam, like a pool or a sheltered pond; turning it off also clears any foam already there. Foam only comes from the ocean waves folding (see [member foam_threshold]) -- bodies disturbing the water don't create it.

Time constant in seconds over which whitecap foam fades once its wave has passed. The foam is kept in a texture that moves with the water rather than the wave shape, so a longer persistence leaves longer streaks behind the crests. The default material also breaks fading foam into lace ([code]foam_breakup[/code], [code]foam_detail_scale[/code] and [code]foam_color[/code] shader parameters), gives its patches crisp, ragged edges ([code]foam_crisp[/code], 0 for soft) and lights their rims as a thin raised skin ([code]foam_relief[/code]).

How squeezed the surface must be before whitecap foam forms: foam is injected where the choppy displacement's area Jacobian drops below this ([code]1[/code] = unsqueezed, [code]0[/code] = folding over). Lower gives fewer whitecaps, needing steeper waves; higher gives more. Depends on [member choppiness] -- without it nothing folds and no foam forms.

If [code]true[/code], [member wind_speed] and [member wind_direction] follow the [WeatherMap3D]'s mean wind at this node. Waves take time to build: the wind the spectrum sees follows the real one over a third of the Shore Protection Manual's growth time for the fetch, g t / U = 68.8 (g F / U^2)^(2/3), in weather time. The spectrum is updated in place, so the waves keep their phases as they grow or turn.
Cell count per side of the local ripple layer's grid. Not required to be a power of two, unlike [member ocean_grid_resolution].

The level settles where the outlets ([method set_outflow]) pass what flows in (the rivers' inflows plus [member catchment_inflow]): the steady state, since a lake takes hours to days to settle. When it moves by more than a centimetre, [member water_level] changes and the rivers leaving and entering rebuild on the new level.

Rendered mesh cells per [member ocean_grid_resolution] cell (1 to 4). A curling breaker needs cells of about a tenth of the wave's height to fold over cleanly; the vertex and path tracing costs grow with the square of this.

Open sea only ([member render_extent] past the simulated square, no [member surface_mesh]): the spacing between the mesh's vertices at the camera, in meters, growing 8% a ring until it reaches the even core's spacing ([member ocean_domain_size] / [member ocean_grid_resolution]), which it keeps out to the core's edge, then the usual growth: finest where it is seen closest (a geometry clipmap's spacing law, in one continuous grid) and nowhere coarser than without it. Where the spacing can carry them, the [member detail_waves] are displaced into the geometry too, so near crests and chop have real silhouettes (also under path tracing). Divided by [member mesh_detail]. [code]0[/code] (the default) keeps an even core over the simulated square; [code]0.03[/code] suits cameras at the water (about twice the vertices; the gain is small: the waves finer than the core's spacing are millimetres high and the per-pixel normal already shows them).

How the surface's normals and whitecap foam are computed, set on the material through its [code]per_pixel_normals[/code] uniform. [constant NORMAL_MODE_PER_PIXEL] uses the exact slopes and displacement derivatives the ocean FFT also produces ([code]ocean_deriv_tex[/code]), so crests shade smoothly and foam follows the folds at any mesh density -- the realistic choice. [constant NORMAL_MODE_PER_VERTEX] takes finite differences of the displaced mesh, so the shading follows the mesh -- softer, faceted at a coarse [member ocean_grid_resolution], for a stylized look.
World-space extent (X, Z) of the FFT ocean layer -- also the size of the rendered [PlaneMesh].

Cell count per side of the FFT ocean layer's grid. Rounded up to the nearest power of two if set otherwise -- the Stockham FFT passes require it. Independent of [member grid_resolution]/[member domain_size] (the ripple layer's own grid) by design: they're two different consumers of "water height" with very different resolution/precision needs, kept architecturally separate rather than forced to share one grid. Up to 1024, with the project setting [code]physics/physx_3d/water/shared_memory_fft[/code] (off until it is timed on a GPU) each step's four transforms run as two dispatches with each line's whole FFT in shared memory instead of one dispatch per butterfly stage; the field is the same. A fetch-limited surface (a lake, or a small [member fetch]) whose spectral peak would span fewer than four cells is given a finer grid, up to 256, so its short waves are not lost.

With a [member render_extent] past the simulated square: if [code]true[/code], the sea out there is open, deep water (full waves, never dry) instead of the square's edge carried outward. Use it when the square follows the camera or player over a coastline: without it, the far sea takes the edge's seabed -- flat, raised to the ground height, with the shore's wet-sand and foam patterns, and [method sample_height] calling it dry.

Raster only, seen from above: the surface mirrors the sky (a small panorama of the environment's sky, baked again every few seconds) and the sun's glitter by the exact Fresnel term, as the path tracer sees it. The sun's highlight uses a GGX lobe at [code]pathtraced_roughness[/code], widened by how fast the wave normals turn across each pixel (geometric specular antialiasing, Tokuyoshi and Kaplanyan 2019), so a far sea gathers its glints into a glitter path instead of flickering. Off, the surface is the unlit tint it was before.

Side length in meters of the rendered surface, centered on the simulation, for open water that runs to the horizon. Past the simulated square the FFT ocean tiles seamlessly (it's periodic), the ripples settle to still water, and the seabed/shoreline values at the square's edge carry on outward; vertex spacing grows with distance, so a few hundred meters costs only a few hundred extra vertices per side. [code]0[/code] (or anything up to [member ocean_domain_size]) renders just the simulated square -- keep it that way for walled water. Ignored with a [member surface_mesh]. Custom materials need to sample the ocean textures with repeat to match (the built-in one does).
Multiplier on the ripple displacement driven by submitted floating-body proxies and impulses. Set lower for small splashes and wakes in a pool; this does not scale the FFT ocean waves.

Lets the ripple layer rest. Above [code]0[/code], once the ripple height stayed within this many meters of [member water_level] everywhere for a few steps, with no sphere (strength not zero) or impulse submitted, the ripple solve, its blit and its readback are skipped until the next [method submit_sphere] / [method submit_impulse]. The ocean, foam and swash keep running. [code]0[/code] solves every step.
Physics layers [member seabed_from_floor]'s rays hit. Only static bodies count; a rigid or character body in the way is skipped.

When on, the still-water depth of each ripple cell is measured on the first physics tick by a ray straight down onto the static bodies in [member seabed_collision_mask], starting 100 m above the water. Waves then travel at the local shallow-water speed, cells where the floor is above the water are dry shore ([method sample_height] returns [code]-INF[/code] and [method is_wet] [code]false[/code] there), and the ocean chop fades out over the shallows (see [member shallow_fade_depth]). Where no floor is found the constant [member depth] applies. Combines with [member surface_mesh]: cells outside its footprint stay dry. The floor is measured once; moving it afterwards needs a property change to re-measure.

Water shallower than this many meters fades the ocean chop out, down to none at the waterline, so the surface meets a beach calmly instead of the chop cutting through the sand. Only has an effect where the depth varies ([member seabed_from_floor] or [member surface_mesh]).

Shore foam: where the still water is shallower than this many meters, each arriving wave crest leaves a thin, lacy foam sheet at the waterline that moves with the water (see [member shore_undertow]), carries on up the swash onto the sand thinning out as it goes (see [member swash_run_up]), and fades out after it (about 1.5 x [member foam_persistence]). Needs a varying depth, so it only appears with [member seabed_from_floor] -- a pool's walls don't get it. [code]0[/code] turns it off, as does [member foam_enabled]. The default material also tints the shallows toward a milky [code]shallow_color[/code] ([code]shallow_tint[/code]) and feathers the surface where it meets the shore; [code]shore_foam_strength[/code] and [code]shore_foam_breakup[/code] tune the sheet. The visible waterline isn't the still-water depth contour: it moves with the arriving waves and slow noise, forming drifting lobes and bays, with a thin bright rim behind it ([code]shore_rim_strength[/code]). The edge is measured in real water depth, independent of [member shallow_fade_depth]: it pulls back over at most [code]swash_reach[/code] meters of depth (pushed in by crests of [code]swash_wave_height[/code]), and [code]shore_edge_softness[/code] is the depth in meters it feathers out over, so the surface only turns clear where the water really is that thin.

Spray from plunging lips: droplets where the lip's edge is thin and fast and where it lands, at rates from the kinetic, wave-crest and trapped-air potentials of Ihmsen et al. (2012). Drawn by one [GPUParticles3D].
The most spray droplets alive at once.

Steady seaward drift (m/s) of the shore foam. The foam moves with the water along the seabed slope at the shallow-water particle velocity -- pushed up the beach under each arriving crest, drawn back between crests (with the local wave height capped by depth-limited breaking) -- and this undertow drags it back out into the water on top of that, so the sheet surges in and slides back out in streaks. [code]0[/code] leaves it rocking in place.

How far plunging breakers curl over: a sheet of water (the lip) is thrown off the crest along a ballistic path over the steep face and lands on the water ahead, then sinks into the bore (Thurey et al. 2007). The lip is separate geometry along the crest lines, so it does not need a fine mesh, and it throws spray (see [member shore_spray]). Whether a beach plunges is set by its slope and the swell's steepness (the surf similarity number, Battjes 1974): gentle beaches spill, moderate ones plunge, steep ones surge, so the curl comes and goes along a varied coast. [code]0[/code] leaves only spilling crests.
The direction (X, Z) the shore waves travel in from the open sea before the seabed turns them. [code]Vector2(0, 0)[/code] uses [member wind_direction].

How much the shore waves' heights vary from wave to wave. At [code]1[/code] each wave has its own height, as in a real sea: the heights follow a Rayleigh distribution (Longuet-Higgins 1952) with [member shore_wave_height] as their rms, in sets of about five bigger waves every twelve or so, so big sets break on the outer bars while small waves run in further before they break (random-wave breaking, Battjes and Janssen 1978, Thornton and Guza 1983). Bigger waves also spill more and smaller ones plunge more. [code]0[/code] makes every wave the same height, so all crests break at the same place.

Height (m, crest to trough) of the shore waves in deep water, before they grow in the shallows: the rms of the individual waves' heights when [member shore_wave_groups] is on (the significant height is about 1.4 times it). The second, longer train is 0.6 of it.
Period (s) of the shore waves: longer swell runs faster, is turned more by the seabed, and breaks further out. The second train is 1.13 times longer, so the two beat into sets.

Swell rolling in onto the shore over the measured seabed ([member seabed_from_floor] or a [member surface_mesh]). Two wave trains whose crests follow a phase field solved over the depth (ray theory), so they slow, turn to follow the depth contours and bunch up in the shallows. They grow as the water shoals (energy flux), break where their height reaches 0.78 of the depth, and run in as white bores up to the waterline. The swash runs them up the sand, as far as the run-up of Stockdon et al. (2006) for the beach slope and the swell. On beaches that plunge the crests curl over first (see [member shore_wave_curl]). Heights vary slowly along the crests, so the waves come in sets. They fade out where the water is deeper than a quarter wavelength, which the FFT ocean carries. Included in [method sample_height]. On enclosed water (a [member surface_mesh]) there is no swell from outside: the height is at most the water's own wind sea (from [member wind_speed] and its fetch), so a still pond has none.

When the surface advances. [constant STEP_MODE_PER_TICK] runs the whole GPU step every physics tick. [constant STEP_MODE_PER_FRAME] records each physics tick (its delta and the spheres / impulses submitted so far) and runs them in ONE step per rendered frame: the ripple layer still takes one sub-step per tick with that tick's bodies (the same ripples), while the FFT ocean (evaluated at the summed time -- the same waves), foam, swash, the texture blits and the height readbacks run once. When the game runs several physics ticks per frame (a high tick rate, or a physics catch-up), this keeps the surface's cost at one step per frame.

Optional water outline: any flat [Mesh] (node-local) whose up-facing triangles' X/Z footprint is the water -- e.g. a disc baked from a [CSGCylinder3D], or a shape modeled elsewhere. Its own vertices are not displaced directly; the footprint is resampled into an even grid clipped to the outline, so a coarse or fan-triangulated mesh still gets vertices to animate everywhere. When set, the ripple grid is fitted to the footprint's bounds ([member domain_size] is ignored) at [member grid_resolution], cells outside it are dry land the waves reflect off, caustics are cut to the water area, and [method sample_height] returns [code]-INF[/code] over dry cells. The FFT ocean layer still covers [member ocean_domain_size] around the same center -- size it to cover the footprint. Unset, the water is the square [member domain_size] / [member ocean_domain_size] plane.
How fast (m/s, vertical) the swash slides back down the sand after a wave has run up. On a 1:14 beach the default 0.12 is a backwash of about 1.7 m/s along the sand.

Swash: the bigger arriving waves (the crests well above the usual ones, so it comes in sets) run up past the still-water line onto the dry sand as a thin film, at most this high (m above still water, not distance along the sand), in tongues that vary along the beach, then slide back down at [member swash_drain_speed]. The run-up grows with the sea state, so a calm lake barely moves. Sand the water has covered stays dark and glossy and dries over [member wet_sand_dry_time]. Needs a varying depth ([member seabed_from_floor]); a pool's walls don't get it. [code]0[/code] turns the run-up off (the sand below the still water still reads wet). The default material draws the film on the sand ([code]swash_film_thickness[/code]) with a ragged, fingered edge ([code]swash_edge_breakup[/code]; [code]shore_detail_scale[/code] sets how fine that, the rim lace and the wet-sand edge are -- [code]foam_detail_scale[/code] only covers the whitecaps and the shore foam sheet) and blends [code]wet_sand_color[/code] over the ground, so it works with any floor material.

With [constant WAVE_SPREADING_DONELAN_BANNER] or [constant WAVE_SPREADING_HASSELMANN], how much of the sea is swell from a distant storm, 0 to 1: Horvath's term, a [code]cos^2s(theta / 2)[/code] factor with [code]s = 16 tanh(wp / w) swell^2[/code], narrows the long waves to nearly parallel crests. 0 is a pure wind sea.

A terrain with holes, such as a [TerrainGenerator3D]. Where a [member seabed_from_floor] ray falls through one of its holes (a cave mouth) and finds nothing, the terrain's own height ([code]get_height[/code]) closes the hole, so the sea never shows through an open hole above the waterline; a static floor under the hole (a sea cave's) counts as usual. The seabed is measured again when the terrain's [code]holes_changed[/code] signal names a rectangle over the simulated square.

The view from under the water, in raster: while the camera is under the surface (or within reach of the waves), a full screen pass fogs what lies under the water by the distance the light travels in it, with the medium of the path traced water ([code]pathtraced_absorption[/code], [code]pathtraced_scattering[/code] and [code]pathtraced_scattering_anisotropy[/code] on [member water_material]), lit by the first visible [DirectionalLight3D] refracted into the water and by the environment's sky. The image splits where the surface crosses the lens, and the surface seen from below shows the world above through Snell's window, refracted, and a mirror of the water past the critical angle (total internal reflection). Surfaces under the water lose the light the water above them absorbed. Off, or with the camera away from the water, nothing extra is drawn. The path tracer needs no setting: it starts the camera's rays in the water by itself (with [code]rendering/pathtracing/refraction[/code] on). Transparent objects under the water are not fogged in raster.
How dark the thin line is where the surface crosses the lens, with [member underwater_enabled]. [code]0.0[/code] draws none.
Mean world-space Y of the surface -- place the node here rather than relying on its own transform, since the rendered mesh and both simulation layers are displaced relative to this baseline.

The material driving the surface mesh's displacement/shading. A default is created automatically if left unset -- assign your own only if you need to customize the look; it must keep sampling [code]ripple_height_tex[/code]/[code]ocean_height_tex[/code] in its vertex shader the same way the default does, or the mesh will stop moving.

Linear height multiplier for the FFT ocean waves. At [code]1.0[/code] they have physical heights for the JONSWAP spectrum at [member wind_speed] and [member fetch] (in meters); below 1 reduces them proportionally, 0 removes the FFT ocean waves. This does not scale local ripple disturbances.
How much larger each wave cascade's tile is than the last.

Number of FFT tiles summed into the ocean. 1 is the single tile of [member ocean_domain_size], which holds no wave longer than the tile, so a strong wind on open water stays short and low. Each extra cascade is a tile [member wave_cascade_ratio] times larger, carrying the band of longer waves (swell), and every tile keeps only waves shorter than a quarter of its size, so none of them shows its repeat. Each extra cascade costs one more FFT ocean on the GPU.

How the ocean's wave energy spreads around the wind direction, from Horvath (2015, "Empirical directional wave spectra for computer graphics"). [constant WAVE_SPREADING_DONELAN_BANNER] (default, Horvath's recommendation) is the measured [code]sech^2[/code] spreading: narrowest at the spectrum's peak, so the dominant waves run with the wind, and wider for shorter and longer waves, so short waves cross. [constant WAVE_SPREADING_HASSELMANN] is Hasselmann et al. (1980)'s [code]cos^2s(theta / 2)[/code] form, wider again for short waves. [constant WAVE_SPREADING_COS2] is the earlier [code]cos^2[/code] spreading with a weak back lobe. [member swell] narrows the first two. Changing it regenerates the spectrum in place.
Time constant (s) for sand uncovered by the swash to dry: the wet darkening fades to about a third over this long. See [member swash_run_up].

If [code]true[/code], the foam threshold is steered each step so the share of sea under whitecaps follows the wind speed as measured at sea (Monahan and O'Muircheartaigh 1980): about 0.1% at 6 m/s, 1% at 10 m/s, 3% at 14 m/s and 8% at 20 m/s, and none in a light breeze. It holds whatever the choppiness, cascades, fetch or spreading. The steering starts from a threshold fitted to the wind (not [member foam_threshold]) and follows the wind as it changes; while new foam is still building up after a start, its reading is scaled up by how far it has filled, so the cover does not overshoot. If [code]false[/code], [member foam_threshold] is used as set.

Multiplies the whitecap cover [member whitecap_auto] aims for. Measured covers at one wind speed spread by about a factor of 3 either way (warmer water and a rising sea foam more), so values between [code]0.3[/code] and [code]3[/code] stay realistic.
Direction (X, Z) the wind blows toward; the FFT ocean waves are aligned with it and travel downwind. Need not be normalized.

Wind speed in m/s driving the FFT ocean layer's spectrum -- higher produces longer, larger waves, up to what [member fetch] and [member depth] allow (a storm needs the sea's real depth: at the default 3 m the long waves are held down). From about 14 m/s (Beaufort 7) fading foam is drawn out into streaks along the wind, fully by 22 m/s; from 9 m/s the crests throw spray (see [member crest_spray]).

constants.constant: Normals and foam per pixel from the ocean FFT's exact derivatives.
Normals and foam per vertex from finite differences of the displaced mesh.
[code]cos^2[/code] spreading about the wind with a weak back lobe.
Donelan-Banner's measured spreading, with Horvath's swell term.
Hasselmann's measured spreading, with Horvath's swell term.
The surface steps every physics tick.
The surface steps once per rendered frame for all of that frame's physics ticks.
